theory.title: Genre, convention and subversion
theory.explanation: Genre is not merely a label: it is a set of historically shaped expectations shared, negotiated and revised by writers, readers and institutions. Conventions may include plot patterns, character roles, settings, stylistic registers and typical resolutions. A work can fulfil them, combine them or make them conspicuous in order to question their assumptions. Subversion is more than surprise: it redirects an established pattern so that its ideological, emotional or formal implications become visible. Genre boundaries are porous and change over time; hybrid works may draw on several traditions without fitting neatly into one category. Strong analysis identifies the convention, demonstrates how the text handles it, and explains the interpretive effect without treating every departure as deliberate rebellion.
theory.tip: Name the convention, locate the textual evidence, then explain whether the work fulfils, revises or subverts the expectation.

patterns.label: Identify the convention
patterns.pattern: Look for recurring plot structures, roles, settings, imagery and stylistic expectations.
examples: The detective is expected to interpret clues and restore order.
The gothic setting makes psychological unease spatially visible.

patterns.label: Distinguish surprise from subversion
patterns.pattern: A reversal becomes subversive when it challenges the values or assumptions carried by the convention.
examples: The apparent villain exposes the institution that created the conflict.

patterns.label: Analyse hybrid forms
patterns.pattern: Explain what each genre contributes and how their combination changes the reader's expectations.
examples: A courtroom drama borrows the uncertainty and atmosphere of a ghost story.

patterns.label: Avoid rigid labels
patterns.pattern: Treat genre as a flexible framework rather than a fixed checklist.
examples: The novel uses crime conventions but refuses the customary final explanation.

items.prompt: What is a genre convention?
options: A recurring feature that shapes expectations within a genre.
A rule that every writer must obey.
A feature found only in poetry.
items.answer: A recurring feature that shapes expectations within a genre.

items.prompt: Which change most clearly subverts a detective convention?
options: The investigation reveals that the institution seeking justice is corrupt.
The detective finds a second clue.
The story takes place in winter.
items.answer: The investigation reveals that the institution seeking justice is corrupt.

items.prompt: What is a hybrid genre?
options: A work combining recognisable features of more than one genre.
A work with no identifiable narrative features.
A story written by two authors.
items.answer: A work combining recognisable features of more than one genre.

items.prompt: Why might a writer exaggerate a familiar trope?
options: To make the convention visible and invite critical reflection.
To ensure readers overlook the convention.
To remove all genre expectations.
items.answer: To make the convention visible and invite critical reflection.

items.prompt: Which claim about genre is most defensible?
options: Genre categories are useful but historically flexible.
Genres never change over time.
Every text belongs to exactly one fixed genre.
items.answer: Genre categories are useful but historically flexible.

items.prompt: A romance ends with the couple separating by choice. What might this do?

items.answer: Challenge the expected resolution and redefine fulfilment.

items.prompt: What distinguishes subversion from mere novelty?

items.answer: It redirects a convention in a way that questions its assumptions.

items.prompt: What should a reader examine in a genre hybrid?

items.answer: How the borrowed conventions interact and alter expectations.

items.prompt: Why can an ending feel unsatisfying by design?

content.passage:
At first glance, Mara's novel appears to follow the familiar pattern of a country-house mystery. A guest disappears during a storm, the doors are locked, and a retired investigator is summoned to question the household. The early chapters carefully plant clues and encourage readers to rank suspects. Yet the investigator gradually discovers that the disappearance was staged by the servants, not to conceal a murder but to expose the owner's plan to sell the estate and dismiss the staff without compensation.

The revelation does not simply replace one culprit with another. It changes the moral centre of the story. The servants have borrowed the machinery of the detective plot—secrecy, false trails and a final disclosure—but redirect it against the social hierarchy that usually remains in the background of the genre. The investigator, who once represented the restoration of order, refuses to identify the organisers.

Some readers may regard the ending as a betrayal of the mystery's promise: no conventional culprit is punished and no stable order is restored. Others may see the refusal as the novel's central achievement. By retaining the genre's pleasures while altering its assumptions about whose interests the law protects, Mara makes the familiar form newly visible. The book remains a mystery, but it asks whether solving a puzzle is the same as delivering justice.

content.audioTranscript: The film begins as a conventional courtroom drama. A defence lawyer appears to be preparing a familiar last-minute revelation, and the audience is encouraged to expect that the evidence will restore public confidence in the legal system. However, the final testimony does not identify a single guilty individual. Instead, it reveals how routine procedures have protected a powerful institution. The director borrows the courtroom genre's suspense and formal confrontation, but refuses its usual promise of individual resolution. This shift does not make the film less coherent; it changes the question at its centre. Rather than asking who broke the rules, the film asks why the rules were designed to benefit some people more than others.
